claims.text: High-temperature oxidation resistance in multiprincipal-element alloys is governed by rapid formation of a thin, adherent, slow-growing oxide scale enriched in protective elements such as Al or Cr.
Al or Cr preferentially diffuses to the alloy surface during high-temperature exposure.
The protective oxide scale limits further oxidation.
Formation of the protective scale stabilizes the alloy microstructure.
The proposed initial alloy has a well-mixed single-phase or dual-phase microstructure and moderate Al or Cr content.
Increasing Al or Cr concentration, or introducing locally enriched regions, will enhance protective surface oxidation.
Selective segregation and oxidation of Al or Cr at grain boundaries and surface regions mediates oxide-scale adhesion and uniformity.
High-temperature diffusion of Al or Cr to the surface produces a coherent, slow-growing Al2O3 or Cr2O3 scale.
A coherent Al2O3 or Cr2O3 scale acts as a physical barrier that reduces oxygen ingress.
The protective scale reduces metal loss.
Reduced oxygen ingress and metal loss preserve the bulk material's structural integrity.
The higher-Al/Cr variant will form a thinner oxide scale than the baseline alloy.
The higher-Al/Cr variant will form a more uniform and adherent oxide scale than the baseline alloy.
The higher-Al/Cr variant will exhibit lower mass gain and less scale spallation than the baseline alloy.
The higher-Al/Cr variant will preserve mechanical integrity better over time than the baseline alloy.
The baseline alloy is expected to develop a less continuous and more rapidly growing oxide scale than the modified alloy under identical conditions.
The proposed mechanism should govern behavior from 800 to 1200 °C under controlled oxygen partial pressures.
Below 800 °C, slower oxidation kinetics may cause deviation from the proposed behavior.
Above 1200 °C, oxide-scale breakdown or volatilization may change the governing mechanism.
